title: Introduction
intro: Lanternly is a deploy console you host yourself. It runs web apps, Docker images and PostgreSQL databases on your own Linux servers, gives each one an HTTPS address, backs them up to any S3 bucket and tells you when something goes down. Think of it as a small Railway or Render that lives on two VMs you control. You pay your cloud provider and nothing else: no seats, no usage meter, no data leaving

s.h: What you can do with it
s.t: Deploy from GitHub. Any repo and branch with a Dockerfile. Images are built on GitHub Actions, every push can deploy itself, and Roll back starts an earlier version without rebuilding. Apps from GitHub Run any Docker image. Docker Hub, ghcr.io or a private registry, pinned to the exact digest that was pulled. Docker images Group services into projects. Each project has its own private network: services find each other by name, and projects can't see each other. Projects S3 storage on your own server. MinIO buckets per project, public or private, linked to apps with the usual S3_* and AWS_* set

s.h: How it works in one picture
s.t: Deployer VM admin.example.com Caddy (HTTPS) Lanternly consoleNext.js + SQLite, queue SSH, clubctl only host key pinned Services VM(s) *.example.com + custom domains Caddy (HTTPS per address) shop-web● Live shop-dbPostgreSQL clubctl · Docker The console never gets a shell on your servers. Its SSH key is locked to one program, clubctl, which accepts a fixed list of commands and checks every argument. More in How it fits together and Security.

Two Ubuntu 24.04 VMs with a static IP and ports 22, 80 and 443 open: a small one for the console (2 GB) and one or more for your services (4 GB or more). Any provider works. A domain whose DNS you control. A GitHub account, if you want to deploy from repos. An S3-compatible bucket, if you want backups.

Lanternly is free software under the GNU Affero General Public License v3.0. Use it for your own work or your clients'. If you run a modified version as a service for other people, you must offer them its source.

title: Quick start
intro: Run the console on your own computer to look around before you set up any servers. Practice mode simulates the services VM and GitHub, so every screen works.

s.t: Node.js 20 or newer and npm Git OpenSSL (to make two random values)

Get the code. git clone https://github.com/thiyagarajanshankar13/lanternly.git cd lanternly npm install Make a settings file. Copy the example and fill in three values. cp .env.example .env.local # .env.local DEPLOYER_SECRET_KEY=<output of: openssl rand -hex 32> DEPLOYER_SETUP_TOKEN=<output of: openssl rand -hex 16> DEPLOYER_FAKE_ENGINE=1 Start it. npm run dev Open http://localhost:3100/admin. Create the first owner. Enter the setup code (your DEPLOYER_SETUP_TOKEN), your name, email and a password, then scan the QR code with an authenticator app (1Password, Google Authenticator, Authy…) and ty
To see the server side work on a machine with Docker (a spare VM or a Linux laptop), run the services setup locally and use names under .localhost: sudo ./agent/setup-clubs-vm.sh
Install on your serversThe real thing: DNS, two VMs and your first deploy. Learn the conceptsWhat servers, projects, services and operations are.

title: Install on your servers
intro: A production install is two Ubuntu VMs: a small one that runs the console, and one or more that run your services. Plan on 15 to 30 minutes.

s.t: You need Notes Deployer VM Ubuntu 24.04, 2 GB RAM, static IP, ports 22, 80 and 443 open. Services VM Ubuntu 24.04, 4 GB RAM or more, static IP, ports 22, 80 and 443 open. You can add more later. A domain One you can add DNS records to. The examples use example.com. An email address For Let's Encrypt certificate notices. Optional A GitHub account (apps from repos), an S3-compatible bucket (backups), an SMTP account (alerts and invites by email). Any provider works: AWS (EC2 or Lightsail), Google Cloud, Hetzner, Vultr, DigitalOcean or your own hardware. If you use AWS, the AWS plugin can create

Add two records at your DNS provider: Name Type Value What it's for admin.example.com A Deployer VM's IP The console *.example.com A Services VM's IP Every service's address, such as shop.example.com The wildcard means new services get an address without a DNS change. You can use any subdomain for the console; admin. is only an example.

Copy the deploy/ folder from the repo to the VM and run the setup script as root: scp -r deploy ubuntu@admin.example.com: ssh ubuntu@admin.example.com cd deploy sudo DEPLOYER_DOMAIN=admin.example.com ./setup-deployer-vm.sh It installs Docker, creates the console's SSH key and secrets in /opt/deployer (never printed again), writes Caddy's config, and prints three things. Keep them for the next steps: the deployer's SSH public key (for the services VM), this VM's host key, a one-time setup code for the first sign-in. To choose your own, pass DEPLOYER_SETUP_TOKEN (16+ letters and digits) to the s

Copy the agent/ folder to the services VM and run its setup with the public key from step 2: scp -r agent ubuntu@<services-vm>: ssh ubuntu@<services-vm> cd agent sudo DEPLOYER_PUBLIC_KEY="ssh-ed25519 AAAA… deployer" \ ACME_EMAIL=you@example.com \ AGENT_ROOT=/opt/lanternly AGENT_NAMESPACE=lanternly \ ./setup-clubs-vm.sh It installs Docker, adds swap, starts Caddy and the clubctl tool, and creates a deployer user whose SSH key can run clubctl and nothing else. At the end it prints this VM's host key. AGENT_ROOT and AGENT_NAMESPACE choose the folder and the container name prefix. They can't be ch

s.h: 4. Sign in for the first time
s.t: Open https://admin.example.com/admin. The certificate is issued on the first visit, so give it a few seconds. Enter the setup code, your name, email and a password (12 characters or more). Scan the QR code with an authenticator app and enter the 6-digit code. On the deployer VM, remove the DEPLOYER_SETUP_TOKEN line from /opt/deployer/.env and restart: cd /opt/deployer && sudo docker compose up -d.

s.h: 5. Connect the console to your server
s.t: Settings → Edit settings: set Domain services live under to example.com. Fill in Outgoing email now if you have an SMTP account (needed for alerts and emailed invites). Servers → Add existing server: the services VM's address for SSH, its public IP, the host key printed by its setup, and its RAM. See Servers. Settings → GitHub → Connect GitHub if you'll deploy from repos. See Connect GitHub. Backups: add your bucket. See Backups. Now create a project and your first service: Projects → New project → New service.
The repo includes workflows that do the server work for you. Fork or copy the repo into your own GitHub account first.

.github/workflows/setup-vm.yml runs steps 2 and 3 over SSH from GitHub Actions. Add these under your repo's Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions, then run it from Actions → Set up a VM: Kind Name Value secret DEPLOYER_VM_SSH_KEY Private key that can SSH to the deployer VM secret DEPLOYER_SETUP_TOKEN A code you make up (16+ letters and digits), typed once at the first sign-in variable DEPLOYER_VM_HOST The deployer VM's address variable DEPLOYER_VM_USER SSH user (default ubuntu) variable DEPLOYER_DOMAIN admin.example.com secret SITES_VM_SSH_KEY Private key that can SSH to the services VM v
.github/workflows/deploy-deployer.yml builds the console image on every push to main and delivers it to the deployer VM. It needs the secret DEPLOYER_VM_SSH_KEY and the variable DEPLOYER_VM_HOST.

title: How it fits together
intro: A few words come up on every page of the console. Here's what they mean and how the pieces talk to each other.

s.t: The console is a Next.js app with a SQLite database, running on the deployer VM behind Caddy. It keeps the list of servers, projects and services, the settings, people and the access log. Secrets it has to keep (app secret settings, registry tokens, bucket keys, SMTP password, two-step sign-in secrets) are encrypted with AES-256-GCM under DEPLOYER_SECRET_KEY. It doesn't run your apps. Every change becomes an operation that it carries out on a server over SSH.

A server is any Ubuntu VM that has been prepared with agent/setup-clubs-vm.sh. That script installs Docker, Caddy and clubctl, and creates a deployer user whose SSH key may only run clubctl. The console saves each server's host key when you add it and refuses to talk to a server that presents a different one. Each server has a memory figure and a limit on how many services it holds, so new services only go where they fit. See Servers.

clubctl is a Bash tool on each server that does the real work, with a fixed list of commands: create, configure, deploy, pause, resume, back up, restore, remove, status and logs, plus database commands (create, stats, credentials, rotate, read-only, upgrade). Each service is a Docker Compose project in its own folder under AGENT_ROOT, with containers named <namespace>-<service>. Caddy on the same server serves every web address over HTTPS and asks Let's Encrypt for a certificate per address.

A project groups the services that make up one product: for example a web app, a worker and a database. Every project runs on one server and has its own Docker network, where each service is reachable by its name (shop-db:5432). Services in one project can't reach services in another. Inside a project, the console draws the services as a diagram in three rows: On the web: apps with a web address. Inside the project: services with no address, such as a worker or Redis. Only the project's other services reach them. Data: the project's PostgreSQL databases and S3 storage. A line runs from each ap

A service is one running thing in a project. The core has four kinds: Kind Comes from Page App from GitHub A repo and branch with a Dockerfile, built on GitHub Actions Apps from GitHub Docker image A ready-made image from any registry Docker images PostgreSQL The official postgres image, managed for you PostgreSQL S3 storage MinIO with buckets, managed for you S3 storage Plugins can add their own kinds (Plugins). Every service has a page with its status, Logs (latest lines or Live, with secrets masked), History (every change with its output and who made it), Pause/Resume and Settings.

Creating, deploying, configuring, pausing, backing up and removing are queued as operations. One operation runs at a time across all servers, so two changes never fight over the same service. App builds run on GitHub, outside that queue, and only the deploy that follows is queued. Each operation's output is kept in the service's History, and Activity → Changes lists every operation with who started it.

Thing Where it lives Services, settings, people, access log Console's SQLite database, /opt/deployer/data App secret settings, tokens, bucket keys Console database, encrypted Database passwords Only on the services VM. Shown in the console on request, and every reveal is logged. Containers, volumes, certificates Services VM, under AGENT_ROOT App images Your registry (ghcr.io for GitHub builds) Backups Your S3 bucket, encrypted with the backup key

title: Servers
intro: Servers are the machines that run your services. Any Ubuntu 24.04 VM you can reach over SSH works, from any cloud or your own hardware.

s.t: On the new VM, copy the repo's agent/ folder and run its setup as root, with the console's SSH public key (shown under Servers and printed when you set up the deployer VM): sudo DEPLOYER_PUBLIC_KEY="ssh-ed25519 AAAA… deployer" \ ACME_EMAIL=you@example.com \ AGENT_ROOT=/opt/lanternly AGENT_NAMESPACE=lanternly \ ./setup-clubs-vm.sh Variable Required Meaning DEPLOYER_PUBLIC_KEY yes The console's SSH public key. It's added to the deployer user, locked to clubctl. ACME_EMAIL yes Email Let's Encrypt writes to about certificates. AGENT_ROOT no Folder where services live. Default /opt/avrosphere. AGEN

Open Servers → Add existing server and fill in: Name: anything that helps you recognise it, such as Frankfurt 1. Address (for SSH): a host name or IP the deployer VM can reach. The user is always deployer, the one the setup made. Public IP: where service domains point. Shown to people adding a custom domain. Host key: the line printed at the end of the setup (ssh-ed25519 AAAA…). The console refuses to talk to a server whose key doesn't match. Memory (MB): the server's RAM. With it set, new services only go on when their memory limits fit. 1 GB is kept for Caddy, the system and the database eng

Every app, image and database has a memory limit (256 MB unless you change it). Creating a service, or giving one more memory, is refused when the memory already given out on its server would go over the server's figure. When every server is full, add another server or raise a limit. A project lives on one server, so all of a project's services share that server's room.

Only the console needs SSH. In your provider's firewall, allow port 22 on services VMs from the deployer VM's IP only (plus your provider's browser console, if you use it). Ports 80 and 443 stay open to everyone for your services.

When a new Lanternly release changes anything under agent/, run the setup script again on each server, or run the Set up a VM workflow (target the services VM). Existing services keep running while it updates. Release notes say when this is needed.

Move or remove its projects and services first. Then open Edit on the server and press Delete this server's record. This only removes it from the console: delete the VM at your provider yourself. Servers made by the AWS plugin can be deleted for real from the console, with a final snapshot.
With the AWS plugin turned on, owners can press Create server to make a new Lightsail VM that sets itself up and joins the list in about 10 minutes. See Create a server.

title: Apps from GitHub
intro: Deploy any repo and branch that has a Dockerfile. Images are built on GitHub Actions, so building costs your servers nothing, and every push to the branch can deploy itself.

s.t: Lanternly talks to GitHub through a GitHub App it creates for you, so there are no keys to copy. Make sure DEPLOYER_URL is the console's public https:// address, so GitHub can send pushes to it. Open Settings → GitHub apps → Connect GitHub. Enter the GitHub organisation or user whose repos you'll deploy, and Builds run in: your copy of the Lanternly repo (for example my-company/lanternly), which holds the build workflow. Press Create GitHub app. GitHub asks you to confirm the new app's name. Install it on your Lanternly repo plus the repos you'll deploy, and you're sent back to the console. Th

s.h: Using a GitHub App you made yourself
s.t: Under Settings → GitHub apps by hand, enter the App ID, the organisation, the repo builds run in, the private key (.pem) and the webhook secret. The app needs: Repository permissions: Contents read, Metadata read, Actions read and write, and optionally Secrets read and write (so the console can save the build secrets itself). Webhook address https://admin.example.com/api/github/webhook, subscribed to the Push event. Without the Secrets permission, add the repo variable APPS_GITHUB_APP_ID and secret APPS_GITHUB_APP_KEY to your Lanternly repo by hand.

A Dockerfile (at the root, or tell the console its path). One web port the app listens on. The app gets PORT as a setting; default 3000. Ideally a health page that answers once the app is ready, such as /health. # A minimal Node app FROM node:20-alpine WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm ci --omit=dev COPY . . EXPOSE 3000 CMD ["node", "server.js"]

Open a project and press New service → App from GitHub. Pick the repository and branch. Only repos the GitHub App is installed on are listed. Give it a short name: its address becomes <name>.example.com and other services in the project reach it by this name. Change the advanced fields if needed: Dockerfile path, port, health page, memory. Add settings and secret settings, one NAME=value per line. Secret ones are stored encrypted, masked in logs and never shown again. Under Databases and storage, tick a database or storage to link, or Create a new PostgreSQL database for it. See Link a databas

The console starts .github/workflows/build-app-image.yml in your Lanternly repo with the app's repo, commit and Dockerfile. The workflow checks out the app repo with a short-lived token from the GitHub App, builds a linux/amd64 image and pushes it to ghcr.io/<owner>/app-<name>:<commit>, keeping the newest 10 versions. The console follows the run and, once it succeeds, deploys that image. A commit that was already built is deployed without building again. A build that doesn't start within 5 minutes, or takes over 45, counts as failed. A failed build never touches the running app. Builds use you

Deploy latest builds the newest commit on the branch and swaps it in. Deploy every push to the branch by itself (in Settings) does the same on each push, through the GitHub webhook. Versions lists each commit that has run. Roll back starts an earlier one in seconds, with no rebuild. Builds lists every build with its result and a link to its GitHub log. Settings changes the branch, Dockerfile, port, health page, memory, settings, secrets, databases and pre-deploy command. Changing the branch or Dockerfile starts a new build. Logs: the latest 200 to 2,000 lines, or Live to watch new ones, with f

A new version must answer its health page (any status under 400) within 2 minutes. If it doesn't, the previous version is started again and the deploy is marked failed, with the output in History. With no health page, "running and not restarting" is enough. While a new version starts, the app is briefly unavailable.

A command that runs once for every new version, with the app's settings and linked databases, before it takes over: usually database migrations. It runs in a throwaway container of the new image on the project's network, with a 15-minute limit. If it fails, the version already running keeps running and the output is on the app's page.

Setting Where it comes from PORT The port you set. You can't override it in settings. Your settings and secrets The app's Settings. DATABASE_URL, PGHOST, PGPORT, PGUSER, PGPASSWORD, PGDATABASE Each linked database (with its prefix, if any). S3_ENDPOINT, S3_BUCKET, keys… (and AWS_*) Each linked storage. See S3 storage. ${{shop-db.DATABASE_URL}} in any value Filled in on the server from a database in the same project.

Apps have no volumes yet: anything written inside the container is lost on the next deploy. Keep data in a database or S3 storage. One build at a time per app. Apps get 1 CPU, a memory limit, a process limit and no-new-privileges.

title: Docker images
intro: Run an image someone has already built, such as nginx, redis or louislam/uptime-kuma, with no GitHub repo involved.

s.t: Open a project and press New service → Docker image. Image: a name and tag such as nginx:1.27, bitnami/redis:7.4, ghcr.io/owner/app:v2 or image@sha256:…, or paste the image's link from hub.docker.com. Pick a version tag rather than latest so every restart runs the same thing. Name: other services in the project reach it by this name. Private image (optional): a registry user name and a read-only access token (on Docker Hub: Account settings → Personal access tokens). Don't use your password. The token is stored encrypted and only used for each pull. Give it a web address: leave it ticked for a

When an image is pulled, the server runs the exact digest it got and the console records it (Pinned to nginx@sha256:…). A tag that's later moved on Docker Hub doesn't change what's running until you ask for it. Pull again fetches the tag again and starts what it points to now. Versions lists each digest that has run, with Roll back. Settings changes the image (pulling and starting the new one), the sign-in, web address, port, health page, memory and settings.

What Image Web address Port Health page Static site or proxy nginx:1.27 yes 80 / Cache for your app redis:7.4 no 6379 empty Uptime dashboard louislam/uptime-kuma:1 yes 3001 / Background worker from your registry ghcr.io/acme/worker:2.3.0 no any empty An app in the same project reaches the Redis above at redis://<name>:6379.
No volumes yet: anything the container writes is lost when it restarts or updates. Keep data in a project database. The image's own start command is used; there's no override.

title: PostgreSQL
intro: Each PostgreSQL database runs in its own container with a volume and a health check, on its project's private network. It has no address on the internet, and its password never leaves the server unless someone asks to see it.

s.t: Open a project and press New service → PostgreSQL database. Give it a name, such as shop-db. Apps reach it at shop-db:5432. Pick a version (16 by default). Under Size and limits, change the memory (default 256 MB) and the disk quota (default 5 GB) if you like. Press Create database. It's ready in a few seconds. The engine is tuned to its memory: shared_buffers is a quarter of it, and max_connections grows with it (20 to 200). Several apps can share one database. Add a second only when you want separate data; its suggested name is then <project>-db-2.

s.h: Link a database to an app
s.t: In the app's Settings, tick the database under Databases and storage. The app restarts with these settings: DATABASE_URL=postgres://…@shop-db:5432/… PGHOST=shop-db PGPORT=5432 PGUSER=… PGPASSWORD=… PGDATABASE=… For a second database, give it a prefix such as ANALYTICS_: the app then gets ANALYTICS_DATABASE_URL and so on. You can also use a database's values inside any setting: REPORTS_URL=${{shop-db.DATABASE_URL}} Both are filled in on the server, so the password never appears in the app's settings in the console.

Connect shows the variables an app needs, with the password hidden. Reveal reads it from the server; every reveal is written to the access log. Back up takes a copy now. Copies are also taken on the backup schedule (see Backups). Pause stops the database; apps using it stop working until Resume. Settings: display name, memory, quota and notes. More → Download a dump: a pg_dump custom-format file you can load on your computer with pg_restore. More → Load a dump: replace the data with a pg_dump -Fc file up to 2 GB. A backup is taken first, and linked apps restart afterwards. More → New password:

s.h: Working on the data from your computer
s.t: The database has no public port. Download a dump and restore it locally: createdb shop_copy pg_restore --no-owner -d shop_copy shop-db.dump To push data in, make a dump with pg_dump -Fc and use Load a dump.

Size is checked every 5 minutes against the quota. At 80% the alert addresses get an email. At 100% the database becomes read-only (apps can read but not write) and another email goes out. Raise the quota in Settings or delete data, and it can write again within 5 minutes. The quota is a soft limit enforced with PostgreSQL's default_transaction_read_only, not a disk limit.
One database per container. No outside port: use dumps. No point-in-time recovery: backups are scheduled dumps.

title: S3 storage (MinIO)
intro: S3 storage gives a project its own S3-compatible bucket storage on its server, next to PostgreSQL, so apps can keep uploads, images and files without an outside service.

s.t: Open a project and press New service → S3 storage (MinIO). Give it a name, such as shop-files. Apps in the project reach it at http://shop-files:9000. Optionally tick Give it a web address (shop-files.example.com, with HTTPS). You need one if browsers should load files from public buckets or signed links, or if you want to use S3 tools from your computer. Name the first bucket (files unless you change it) and choose whether anyone with the link may read it, then press Create. Each storage is its own container running a patched MinIO image (pinned to the digest it pulled), with 256 MB of memory

A storage holds up to 20 buckets. Under Buckets on its page: Add a bucket: 3 to 63 lowercase letters, digits and hyphens. Who can read: Apps only (they use the key, or hand out signed links) or Anyone with the link (for images on a website). A public bucket's files are at https://shop-files.example.com/<bucket>/<file>. Remove: only an empty bucket is removed. Delete its files first, from an app or with an S3 tool. File counts and sizes per bucket are checked every 5 minutes.

In the app's settings, under Databases and storage, tick the storage and pick a bucket. The app restarts with: S3_ENDPOINT=http://shop-files:9000 S3_PUBLIC_URL=https://shop-files.example.com S3_REGION=us-east-1 S3_BUCKET=uploads S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID=… S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=… S3_FORCE_PATH_STYLE=true With no prefix, the app also gets the AWS_* names (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_REGION…) that AWS SDKs read, so most S3 libraries work without code changes. For a second storage or bucket, give it a prefix such as MEDIA_: the app gets MEDIA_S3_ENDPOINT and so on. One value in any settin

Keys are made on the server and never stored by the console. Connect shows the values an app needs; Show the secret key reads it over SSH once, and each time is written to the access log. New keys rotates the app key and restarts the apps that use it.

s.h: Using S3 tools from your computer
s.t: With a web address turned on, any S3 tool can use it as the endpoint with the values from Connect: aws s3 ls s3://uploads --endpoint-url https://shop-files.example.com mc alias set shop-files https://shop-files.example.com KEY SECRET Without a web address, only apps in the project can reach the storage.

Each storage has a soft quota (10 GB by default, under Settings). The alert addresses get an email at 80% and 100%. Writes never stop: the server's disk is the real limit, so keep an eye on it on the Servers page.

Storage is backed up with your other services to your backup bucket: every bucket's files, stored once per content and encrypted. Restoring puts the whole storage back as it was, or makes a copy. Remove this storage (owners) takes a final backup, then moves its data aside on the server.

Connect, Buckets, About (address, apps using it, size against the quota), Backups, Logs and History, plus Settings for memory (changing it restarts the storage for a few seconds), quota, web address and notes. On the project diagram, storage sits in the bottom row (now called Data) with its own icon, and apps have lines to the storage they use.

title: Domains and HTTPS
intro: Every service with a web address gets <name>.example.com with a free HTTPS certificate, and you can add as many custom domains as you like.

s.t: Under Settings → Edit settings → Domain services live under, set the domain your wildcard DNS record points at (for example example.com). A service named shop then gets shop.example.com. Names like www, admin and api are reserved; add more under Branding → More reserved names. A service's name, and so its base address, can't change after it's created. Add a custom domain instead.

At the domain's DNS provider, add one record: for a subdomain such as www.shop.com or app.shop.com: a CNAME to the service's address (shop.example.com); for a bare domain (shop.com): an A record to the server's public IP. The service's page shows both values. On the service's page, open More → Custom domain (or Add a custom domain), enter the domain and press Add domain. The console checks the record is in place first. The server asks Let's Encrypt for a certificate within a minute. That only works once DNS points at the server, so add the record first. A bare domain and www. are two addresses
The first custom domain becomes the service's main address. With several, press Make main to choose. The example.com address keeps working.

If a domain was added before its DNS pointed at the server (with Add anyway, or the record changed later), visitors see a security error and the server waits longer before each new try. Once the record is right, press Retry HTTPS under Addresses and the server asks again straight away. The output lists which addresses have a certificate. DNS changes can take a few minutes to an hour to appear. If your own computer still shows the old site, it's remembering the old DNS record: try another device or mobile data, or wait. Check the record from anywhere with dig +short www.shop.com.

Certificates are issued per address. Let's Encrypt allows about 50 new certificates a week per registered domain, so creating many services under one base domain in a single week can hit that limit. Monitoring warns 14 and 3 days before any certificate runs out (renewal is automatic, so a warning means something is wrong).

The console's domain is set when you set up the deployer VM (DEPLOYER_DOMAIN). To move it, point the new name's DNS at the deployer VM and run setup-deployer-vm.sh again with the new DEPLOYER_DOMAIN: it rewrites Caddy's config and DEPLOYER_URL and reloads Caddy. Then restart the console with cd /opt/deployer && sudo docker compose up -d. If you use Connect GitHub, connect again so GitHub sends pushes to the new address.

title: Backups
intro: Backups go to any S3-compatible bucket you own, encrypted with a key only you hold before they leave the console. Each service has its own schedule, and backups are also taken before upgrades, restores and removals.

s.t: The console collects each part of a backup from the server over its SSH connection, encrypts it with the backup key and uploads it. Your servers never see the bucket keys and never talk to the bucket. Files are stored once per content, so frequent backups mostly cost the size of the database dump. Optionally, the image each backup needs is saved once in the bucket too, so a restore still works if the image is deleted from its registry. Until a bucket is set up, each server keeps a nightly database copy on its own disk (14 days).

Create a private bucket in any S3-style store: AWS S3, Lightsail object storage, Backblaze B2, Cloudflare R2, Wasabi or MinIO. Pick a region near your servers. Create an access key that can read and write that bucket. On Backups → Set up the bucket, fill in the bucket name, region and both key parts. For anything other than AWS, open Advanced → Storage address and enter the store's S3 endpoint (for example https://<account>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com). Choose the schedule new services get and press Save, then Test the bucket: it writes a test file, reads it back and deletes it. A Save the backup

Each service has its own schedule, under Backups on its page (Change the schedule): Daily at the hour you pick, in the default time zone. New services get daily at 2am, kept 30 days, unless you change the default. Frequent: every hour or every 6 hours, with its own keep period. A frequent backup is skipped when the daily one has just run. Always: before every database upgrade, before every restore and before a service is removed. Back up now takes one by hand. Changing a keep period applies to existing backups too. The newest good backup of a running service is never deleted, whatever its age.

The Backups page lists every service's last good backup, how many it has, the space they use and a flag when one failed or is overdue, plus the bucket's total use. When a scheduled backup fails, or none has worked for twice the usual gap, an email goes to the alert addresses, and another when backups work again.

On the service's page, under Backups, open Restore for the backup you want. Only owners can restore, with the service's name and a fresh two-step code. Put this service back: a safety backup is taken first, then the data is replaced. If the service doesn't start afterwards, it's put back as it was. Its addresses and settings stay as they are now. Make a copy at a new address: creates a separate service from the backup, so you can look at old data without touching the live one. Remove it when you're done. For a database, the copy is a new database in the same project. Restores are listed in the

If the deployer VM is lost, scripts/backup-tool.mjs in the repo reads the bucket directly with the backup key and the bucket keys, checking every checksum: export BACKUP_KEY=… BUCKET=my-backups REGION=eu-central-1 export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=… AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=… node scripts/backup-tool.mjs list node scripts/backup-tool.mjs fetch <service folder> <backup> ./out A database backup comes out as database.dump, which you load with pg_restore --no-owner.

Because backups live in your bucket, moving is: set up a services VM at the new provider, add it under Servers, then restore each service as a copy on the new server and move your domains. The old server can then be emptied and removed.

title: Monitoring
intro: Every service with a web address is checked every few minutes, and you can add sites hosted anywhere else. Lanternly records whether each one is up, how fast it answers, its version and when its certificate runs out, and emails you when something changes.

s.t: Each check asks <site>/api/health if the site has one, else its home page (or the health page you set). For each site the Monitoring page shows: Status: Up, Down, or Retrying (one check failed; a site only counts as down after two failures in a row). Speed: how long it took to answer. Up, 7 days: the share of checks that passed in the last week. Version: if the health page reports one ({"version": "1.4.0"}). Certificate: days until the HTTPS certificate runs out. Sites that are down are listed first, and the page refreshes by itself. Paused services and services still being created aren't chec

Under Watch a site hosted elsewhere, type its address, such as https://www.example.org. Optionally give it a name. Press Add and check. The first check runs straight away. Nothing needs installing on that site. Lanternly only watches it; it can't restart or change a site it doesn't run. Private and loopback addresses are refused, so monitoring can't be used to probe your own network.

A site can also report how many users it has. If it exposes /api/health/stats behind a key, open it on the Monitoring page, scroll to Settings, set the same value as the site's STATS_API_KEY under Key for user numbers and press Save. Lanternly reads the numbers once an hour, only counts, never names or emails.

Labels sort sites into groups, such as Production and Staging, or one label per client. Press Edit at the end of a site's row. Under Labels, pick a label or type a new one and press Enter. A site can have several. Press Save. Each label gets its own table with its own up, down and behind counts; sites without one are under No label. Group by labels / One list switches between tables and a single list with tags. Click label tags to show only some groups. The browser address keeps your choice, so you can bookmark it. Labels in the toolbar renames, recolours, orders and deletes labels.

Click a site for uptime over 24 hours and 7 days, its usual speed and the latest checks (kept 14 days). From there you can rename it, change its address or labels, pause checks and alerts during planned work, or stop watching it.

An email goes out when: a site is down (two failed checks in a row), it's back up, with how long it was down, a certificate has 14 days left, and again at 3 days. Under Alerts, type who should get them (comma-separated). Empty means every owner. Save and send a test email checks delivery. You can also set how often sites are checked (1 to 60 minutes). The same addresses get database quota, backup and (with the AWS plugin) cost alerts. All of them need the outgoing email account under Settings.

title: People and access
intro: Everyone signs in with a password and an authenticator app. Owners decide who else can sign in, and which projects and services each person can see and change.

s.t: Owner Operator Viewer Status, versions, addresses, monitoring, logs (latest and live), builds everything their services their services Deploy, restart, pause, roll back, settings, domains, back up now, backup schedule yes their services no Add apps and databases to a project; database password, upgrade and dumps yes their whole projects no Create, remove or restore services; make, delete or move projects; servers, settings, plugins, backups page, people, access log yes no no A service that isn't on someone's list doesn't exist for them: it's not on any list, and its page answers "not found".

Each operator or viewer has a list: Everything, including services added later, or Whole projects: everything in the projects you tick, including services added to them later. An operator of a project can also add apps and databases to it. Single services you tick. Changes apply at once. There's always at least one owner, and you can't remove or demote yourself.

Open People → Invite someone, type their name and email, pick a role and what they can see. Press Invite. Copy the link from the bottom of the page and send it, or tick Also email them the link once outgoing email is set up. They open the link, choose a password and scan the QR code with an authenticator app. The link works once, for 72 hours. If it runs out, open them under People and press Make a new invite link.

Press Edit beside a person to change their name, role or list, or: Reset two-step sign-in for a lost phone: they set it up again at their next sign-in. Suspend: signed out at once and can't sign in; their access is kept for when you let them back. Remove: type their email to confirm. Your account in the side menu shows what you can do and lets you change your password (you're signed out everywhere and sign in again with the new one).

Activity → Access log (owners only) records sign-ins and failed sign-ins, invites and access changes, changes to settings, servers, GitHub, the backup bucket and plugins, backup key reveals, database password reveals, restores, and who read which service's logs (one line per person per service per hour). Each line has the time and IP address, and the log is kept for a year. Changes to services themselves are under Activity → Changes, with who made each one and its output.

title: Security
intro: Lanternly is built so that a compromised console can do as little damage as possible, and so that secrets stay where they belong.

s.h: The console can't get a shell
s.t: The console's SSH key is added to the deployer user on each server with a forced command: agent/clubctl-ssh. That wrapper only runs clubctl with a fixed set of commands, each argument checked, and refuses anything else (status; rm -rf / is rejected). The deployer user's sudo rule allows that one program and nothing more.
Each server's SSH host key is saved when you add it. The console refuses to talk to a server that presents a different key, so a swapped or impersonated server gets nothing.

Secret How it's kept App secret settings, registry tokens, bucket keys, SMTP password, GitHub App key, two-step secrets Encrypted with AES-256-GCM under DEPLOYER_SECRET_KEY in the console database. Database and storage passwords Generated on the server and never stored by the console. Reading one is an audited action. Backups Encrypted with the backup key before upload. Servers never see the bucket. Logs Secret settings and anything that looks like a password or token are masked before logs leave the console. Back up DEPLOYER_SECRET_KEYIt's in /opt/deployer/.env. Without it, the encrypted valu

Everyone needs a password (12+ characters) and an authenticator code. There is no way to turn two-step sign-in off. Sessions are kept on the server and end at once when someone is suspended or removed, or changes their password. Restores and backup key reveals ask for a fresh two-step code, with a limit on wrong tries.
Every server action and admin API route checks the person's access (src/lib/access.ts). A test fails if one forgets. A service someone may not see answers 404, not 403, so its existence doesn't leak.

Databases have no published port. Services in one project can't reach another project's services. Monitoring refuses private and loopback addresses. The GitHub webhook checks GitHub's signature with a constant-time compare. Recommended: allow SSH on services VMs only from the deployer VM.

Remove DEPLOYER_SETUP_TOKEN from /opt/deployer/.env after the first sign-in. Limit port 22 on services VMs to the deployer VM's IP; on the deployer VM, to your own IPs. Keep the backup key and DEPLOYER_SECRET_KEY in a password manager. Use a bucket with a different provider from your servers. Give people the lowest role that works, scoped to their projects. Apply OS security updates on the VMs (unattended-upgrades is Ubuntu's default). Upgrade to the newest Lanternly release: only it gets security fixes.

Please don't open a public issue. Use Report a vulnerability on the repo's Security tab, with what you found, how to reproduce it and what an attacker could do. We aim to answer within 5 working days and fix confirmed problems within 30. Full policy: SECURITY.md. Out of scope: anything that needs an owner account, root on a VM, problems in the apps you deploy, and denial of service against one install unless it's easy to trigger without signing in.

title: Settings and branding
intro: Settings holds the defaults for every service. Only owners can open it.

s.t: Domain services live under: the domain your wildcard DNS points at, such as example.com. A service named shop gets shop.example.com. Nothing can be created until it's set. Default time zone: used for backup schedules and dates.

An SMTP account the console sends through: monitoring, database, backup and cost alerts, invites and tests. Fill in the SMTP server, user name, password (stored encrypted) and sender address. Any provider works (Amazon SES, Postmark, Mailgun, your own mail server). Until it's set, alerts aren't emailed and pages say so.

Name: shown in the side menu, on the sign-in page and in the authenticator app. Line under the name (optional): also ends every page title. Logo address (optional): an image URL. Empty shows the built-in mark. Locale: how dates and numbers are written, such as en-US, en-GB or de-DE. More reserved names: names no service may take, on top of www, admin, api and the like.
The GitHub App used to build and deploy apps: Connect GitHub creates one for you, or enter one by hand. Also the default memory limit per app. See Connect GitHub.

Manage plugins lists the installed plugins with what each adds; turn them on or off, and open a plugin's own settings. Turning a plugin off hides what it adds but never stops anything it created. See Plugins.
Who can sign in is on its own page in the side menu. See People and access.

title: Plugins
intro: Plugins add service kinds, pages, settings and timers without the core knowing about them. Lanternly ships with one, Amazon Web Services, and you can write your own.

s.t: Owners open Settings → Plugins → Manage plugins. Each plugin says what it adds and what turning it off does. A fresh install starts with every plugin off. Turning a plugin off hides its pages, menu items and buttons, but never stops what it created: services keep running, backed up and monitored, and servers it made stay listed so they can still be followed and deleted.
Amazon Web ServicesCreate and delete Lightsail servers from the console, and see what AWS charges in your currency, with budget alerts and a per-project estimate.

A plugin lives in src/plugins/<id>/. The AWS plugin (src/plugins/aws/) is a complete example. Describe it. Create src/plugins/<id>/plugin.ts exporting a DeployerPlugin (typed in src/plugins/types.ts): id, name, description, icon, the pages it owns, optional side-menu items ({ href, label, icon, group }) and service kinds. Register it. Add one line to src/plugins/installed.ts. If it has server code (timers, service kind steps, a latestVersion check), add a line to installed-hooks.ts; if it has React parts (a settings card, Servers or Services page parts, a service's page), to installed-parts.ts

The core never imports a plugin directly. It goes through two files: src/plugins/server.ts: server-side hooks, such as startPlugins() (timers, called at start-up), projectCosts(), serverBusy() and serviceKind() for create, configure and upgrade steps of a plugin's service kind. src/plugins/parts.ts: React parts, such as serversPageParts() (toolbar, notices, footer), parts for the Services page, a service kind's page and its list cells.

Every line in a shared file that mentions a plugin ends with a comment plugin:<id>, and longer stretches sit between plugin:<id>:start and plugin:<id>:end. A file whose first line carries the tag belongs to the plugin. This lets scripts/export-core.mjs produce a copy without a given plugin (useful for keeping a plugin private), so keep the tags when you edit those lines. import { awsPlugin } from './aws/plugin' // plugin:aws

title: Amazon Web Services plugin
intro: The AWS plugin adds two things for people who host on Amazon: Create server, which makes a Lightsail VM that sets itself up and joins your servers, and Costs, which shows what AWS charges in the currency you choose. Everything else in Lanternly works on AWS without this plugin: EC2 or Lightsail VMs added by hand, S3 or Lightsail buckets for backups. The plugin only adds convenience.

s.t: Settings → Plugins → Manage plugins → Amazon Web Services. It's off on a new install. Turning it off later hides Costs, Create server, AWS for new servers and Check Lightsail, and stops the cost timer. Servers it made stay listed and can still be deleted. The plugin uses two separate AWS keys, each with the least it needs: Key Used for Can it change things? Costs key (for example IAM user lanternly-costs) Reading Cost Explorer, Free Tier and Lightsail plan prices Only the one AWS budget the console keeps Servers key (for example lanternly-provision) Creating and deleting Lightsail VMs Only VMs

Costs in the side menu (owners only) shows: This month so far, the forecast for the month and last month. What you pay each day for the last 31 days (UTC days, as AWS counts them; today is still counting). By AWS service after credits, and a breakdown of Lightsail: VMs, buckets, static IPs, data transfer, snapshots, databases and load balancers. Credits and free tier: charges, credits and what you actually paid each month, credits left and when they'll run out at the current pace, and free tier use this month. Each project, a month (estimate): each server's plan price shared between the projec

In the AWS console, Billing → Cost Explorer: turn it on if it isn't. The first numbers take up to a day. Account → IAM user and role access to Billing information: turn it on. IAM → Users → Create user (for example lanternly-costs, no console access). Add the policy below as an inline policy. On the user, Security credentials → Create access key ("Application running outside AWS"). On Costs → Connect AWS, paste both parts and the Lightsail region your servers are in (for example eu-central-1), and save. { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "ReadCosts", "Effect": "Allow", "Action"

AWS bills in US dollars. Under Costs → Budget and alerts → Show money in, pick one of: Code Currency USD US dollar (default; shown exactly as AWS bills) EUR, GBP Euro, pound sterling AUD, NZD, CAD, SGD Australian, New Zealand, Canadian and Singapore dollars INR Indian rupee Other currencies are converted at the day's European Central Bank rate (from the free Frankfurter service). To match your invoice exactly, type the rate from your AWS invoice instead. If the rate service can't be reached, the last known rate is used; failing that, the page shows US$ and says so. Changing the currency fetche

Set a Monthly budget (empty = no budget, spike alerts only). The alert addresses from Monitoring get an email: at 50%, 80% and 100% of the budget (each once a month), when the forecast goes over the budget (once a month), on a spike: yesterday cost more than twice the 7-day average, by a meaningful amount (about US$1.30 or more), when credits will run out or expire within 30 days. Without an outgoing email account, press Save as AWS budget: AWS creates a budget named avro-deployer-monthly and emails the same people at 80% and 100% actual, and 100% forecast.

AWS shows credits used, but has no API for how much of a credit code (AWS Activate, a promotion) is left. Copy the balance from AWS Billing → Credits into Credits left (US$) with its expiry date; credits used from that day on are taken off it. Accounts on the AWS free plan are read automatically.

Owners can make a new Lightsail VM from Servers → Create server. It takes about 10 minutes and needs nothing from you after you press the button. Give it a name, such as Frankfurt 2. The page shows the name it gets in Lightsail. Pick a size. Each shows its monthly price in your Costs currency and what all your Lightsail plans would cost with it: Size Holds about 1 GB one small app, never shared 2 GB 2 services' worth of room 4 GB 5 8 GB (default) 10 16 GB 20 Each size uses the cheapest current Lightsail Linux plan with that much memory and an IPv4 address. Press Create server and watch the ste

The limit: at most 5 servers made by the console, unless you raise it under AWS for new servers. The budget: when the new server would take your monthly Lightsail plans over the Costs budget, tick Go over the budget to make it anyway. Setup: the page lists anything missing: the key, an https:// DEPLOYER_URL, the certificate email, the console's SSH key.

s.h: Set up AWS for new servers (once)
s.t: Open Servers → AWS for new servers and fill in: An access key for its own IAM user (not the costs key, which is refused), with the policy below. The region (and zone) new servers go in. The deployer's public IP: the only address allowed on SSH to new servers. Most servers the console may make (default 5). The email for HTTPS certificate notices. Optional: a GitHub user and package token (read:packages) so new servers can pull private ghcr.io images. The screen shows the exact policy for your region. It looks like this (for eu-central-1): { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "Read

Only servers the console made can be deleted from here, and only once nothing is on them. Open Edit on the server, type its name and press Delete this server. The console takes a last snapshot, deletes the VM and releases its static IP. The snapshot is kept 14 days (listed under Snapshots of deleted servers) so you can still make a VM from it in Lightsail, then deleted.

Once a day the console looks for Lightsail VMs tagged as its own that aren't on the Servers page, and deletes expired snapshots. Press Check Lightsail to do it now. Stray VMs are shown on the page and emailed to the alert addresses, because they still cost money.
With DEPLOYER_FAKE_ENGINE=1 and no key, Costs shows steady made-up numbers in the shape AWS sends, and Create server runs against a pretend Lightsail.

title: Configuration reference
intro: Most configuration lives in the console's Settings. A few values are environment variables, set in /opt/deployer/.env on the deployer VM (or .env.local when running locally).

s.t: Variable Meaning DEPLOYER_SECRET_KEY Required. 32 random bytes as hex (openssl rand -hex 32). Encrypts the secrets the console stores. Losing it loses them. Made by the setup script. DEPLOYER_URL The console's own address, such as https://admin.example.com. Used in links, the authenticator label and the GitHub webhook. Must be public https:// for Connect GitHub and Create server. DEPLOYER_SETUP_TOKEN One-time code for creating the first owner at /admin/setup. Remove it once the owner exists. DEPLOYER_DATA_DIR Where the SQLite database and uploads live. /data in the container (/opt/deployer/dat

Each background timer can be stopped with off, for example on a second copy of the console used for testing. Variable Stops DEPLOYER_MONITOR=off Monitoring checks and alerts DEPLOYER_BACKUPS=off Scheduled backups and clean-up DEPLOYER_DB_WATCH=off Database size and quota checks DEPLOYER_COSTS=off AWS plugin: the daily cost fetch DEPLOYER_PROVISION=off AWS plugin: server create/delete steps and the daily Lightsail check

Variable Meaning DEPLOYER_MONITOR_ALLOW_PRIVATE Lets monitoring check private and loopback addresses. For local testing only. DEPLOYER_AGENT_DIR AWS plugin: where the agent/ files are that new servers get. Default ./agent in the image.

For deploy/setup-deployer-vm.sh: Variable Meaning DEPLOYER_DOMAIN Required. The console's domain, such as admin.example.com. DEPLOYER_SETUP_TOKEN Optional. Your own first sign-in code (16+ characters, no spaces or quotes). Otherwise one is made up and printed. When starting the console with Docker Compose in /opt/deployer, DEPLOYER_IMAGE names the image to run.

For agent/setup-clubs-vm.sh: Variable Meaning DEPLOYER_PUBLIC_KEY Required. The console's SSH public key. ACME_EMAIL Required. Email for Let's Encrypt notices. AGENT_ROOT Folder for everything on the server. Default /opt/avrosphere. AGENT_NAMESPACE Prefix of container names, labels and shared networks. Default avrosphere. GHCR_USER, GHCR_TOKEN Optional login for pulling private images from ghcr.io.

Workflow Secrets and variables setup-vm.yml (Set up a VM) See Install → Set up a VM. deploy-deployer.yml (Deploy the deployer) secret DEPLOYER_VM_SSH_KEY, variable DEPLOYER_VM_HOST (and DEPLOYER_VM_USER, DEPLOYER_VM_HOST_KEY). build-app-image.yml (app builds) variable APPS_GITHUB_APP_ID, secret APPS_GITHUB_APP_KEY. Saved for you by Connect GitHub. ci.yml None: type check, tests and build on pull requests.

What Where Console (dev) http://localhost:3100/admin Console on the VM /opt/deployer: .env, docker-compose.yml, Caddyfile, data/, keys/ Services on a server <AGENT_ROOT>: agent.conf, one folder per service, Caddy config Open ports 80 and 443 on both VMs; 22 on services VMs from the deployer VM only

title: Upgrading Lanternly
intro: An upgrade has two parts: the console on the deployer VM, and clubctl on each services VM when a release changes it. Your services keep running throughout.

s.t: Read the release notes. They say when servers need the new clubctl, and about any new required setting. Copy /opt/deployer/data somewhere safe (it's small). The console's database is migrated forward on start and can't be migrated back.
If you use the Deploy the deployer workflow, merge the new release into your copy's main branch. The workflow builds the image and restarts the console.

cd lanternly git pull sudo docker build -t deployer . cd /opt/deployer && sudo env DEPLOYER_IMAGE=deployer docker compose up -d On start, the console applies any new database migrations (they're numbered and only ever added, never edited). Operations that were running when it stopped are picked up again.

When the release notes say so, run the setup again on each services VM with the new agent/ folder (same values as the first time), or run the Set up a VM workflow for it. Running containers aren't recreated. sudo DEPLOYER_PUBLIC_KEY="ssh-ed25519 AAAA… deployer" \ ACME_EMAIL=you@example.com ./setup-clubs-vm.sh Servers keep their AGENT_ROOT and AGENT_NAMESPACE from agent.conf, so you don't need to pass them again. Servers made by the AWS plugin are updated the same way (point the workflow at the server's address).

Normal OS updates are fine. For a reboot, the containers restart by themselves. For a bigger change, such as a new Ubuntu release, it's often easier to create a fresh server, restore each service onto it as a copy, move domains and remove the old one.

title: Troubleshooting
intro: Most problems show up in a service's History, where every operation keeps its full output. Start there.

s.t: The server presented a different SSH host key from the one saved. If you rebuilt the VM, that's expected: open Servers → Edit and paste the new key printed by the setup script. If you didn't, stop and find out why before going further.
Check port 22 on the server allows the deployer VM's IP. Check the setup ran with the right DEPLOYER_PUBLIC_KEY (the one under Servers). The SSH user is always deployer, not ubuntu or root.
The memory already given out on that server plus the new service's limit is over the server's figure. Lower some memory limits, raise the server's figure if it really has more RAM, or add a server.
The server has an older clubctl than the console expects. Run the services setup again (see Update clubctl).

Open Builds → GitHub log. The usual causes: the Dockerfile path is wrong, the GitHub App isn't installed on the repo, or the Lanternly repo is missing the build secrets (the GitHub page says so). A failed build never touches the running version.
The build workflow didn't start within 5 minutes. Check that .github/workflows/build-app-image.yml is on your copy's default branch and that Actions are enabled there.

Check Deploy every push to the branch by itself is ticked in the app's Settings. DEPLOYER_URL must be the console's public https:// address. In the GitHub App's settings, Advanced → Recent deliveries shows whether GitHub reached it.

s.h: The new version is rolled back
s.t: It didn't answer its health page within 2 minutes. Check the port the app listens on matches the service's port (the app gets PORT), the health page returns a status under 400, and look at Logs for crashes. A failed pre-deploy command also keeps the old version; its output is in History.

The DNS record must point at the server before a certificate can be issued. Fix it, then press Retry HTTPS. dig +short <domain> should show the server's IP (or the CNAME then the IP). Let's Encrypt allows about 50 new certificates per registered domain per week. If you hit it, wait, or spread services over more than one base domain.

If alerts or invites don't arrive, open Monitoring → Alerts → Save and send a test email. The error says whether the SMTP server, port or sign-in is wrong. Check spam folders and that the sender address is allowed by your provider.

Press Test the bucket on the Backups page; it explains a wrong key, region or endpoint. For R2, B2, Wasabi or MinIO, the Storage address under Advanced must be set. The key needs to list, read, write and delete in the bucket.
The database reached its quota. Raise it under the database's Settings or delete data; writes come back within 5 minutes.

AccessDenied on Costs: the key lacks the policy, or "IAM user and role access to Billing information" is off in the account settings. "Cost Explorer has no data yet": turn it on under Billing; the first numbers take up to 24 hours. Create server stuck at booting: the VM never called back. Check DEPLOYER_URL is public https://, then Discard and try again.

cd /opt/deployer sudo docker compose ps sudo docker compose logs --tail 200 app sudo docker compose logs --tail 100 caddy If you've lost every owner's two-step device, another owner can reset it under People. If there's no other owner, ask for help in a GitHub issue (don't post secrets).

One operation runs at a time across all servers (app builds run on GitHub, outside that queue). While a new app version starts, the app is briefly unavailable. Apps and images have no volumes yet; data belongs in a database. Certificates are per address, within Let's Encrypt's weekly limits. Default server folder and container prefix are /opt/avrosphere and avrosphere unless you set AGENT_ROOT and AGENT_NAMESPACE.

title: Contributing
intro: Bug reports, fixes, docs and new plugins are all welcome. For anything bigger than a small fix, open an issue first so we can agree on the approach.

s.t: git clone https://github.com/thiyagarajanshankar13/lanternly.git cd lanternly cp .env.example .env.local # DEPLOYER_SECRET_KEY, DEPLOYER_SETUP_TOKEN, DEPLOYER_FAKE_ENGINE=1 npm install npm run dev # http://localhost:3100/admin

s.h: Before you send a pull request
s.t: npm run typecheck npm test npx next build Add or change tests with the code. Tests live in tests/, a plugin's in tests/plugins/<id>/. tests/contract.test.ts snapshots every clubctl call and the settings sent with it. A changed snapshot changes what live servers receive: update it only on purpose (npx vitest run -u), with the matching change to agent/clubctl, and say so in the pull request. Every server action and admin API route must call an access check (requireOwner, requireSite and friends in src/lib/guards.ts). tests/access.test.ts fails otherwise. Database changes are a new entry at the e

Path What's there src/app/admin/ The console's pages and server actions src/lib/ Operations queue, SSH runner, access rules, backups, monitoring, Postgres, apps src/plugins/ Plugin registry and the AWS plugin agent/ clubctl, its SSH wrapper, the services VM setup and Compose files deploy/ Deployer VM setup and its Compose file scripts/ backup-tool.mjs, export-core.mjs .github/workflows/ CI, app builds, Set up a VM, Deploy the deployer

We use the Developer Certificate of Origin instead of a CLA. Add a Signed-off-by line to each commit: git commit -s -m "Fix the backup retry" By contributing you agree your work is released under the GNU AGPL v3.

The docs are plain HTML on the gh-pages branch. Each page's text is a fragment in docs-src/pages/; the menu, search index and page frame are added by a small script with no dependencies: git checkout gh-pages # edit docs-src/pages/<page>.html node docs-src/build.mjs # open docs/index.html in a browser, then commit docs-src/ and docs/ Every page has an Edit this page on GitHub link at the bottom.
